beats.narration: Chapter 25 covers targeted therapies, the drugs built to hit one molecule rather than every dividing cell. The chapter carries 288 sentences. Forty-five of them were flagged for verification, and 22 of those fell inside my scope, the ones marked false, flagged, or sent up for expert review. I worked 12 editorial findings on top of that.

beats.narration: Of the 22 assertions I reviewed, 14 need revision and 8 are approved as written. That is a higher correction rate than Chapter 23, and I think the subject explains it. Almost every sentence in this chapter names a drug, a target, a trial or an approval, and each one of those is a fact with a record behind it that either matches or does not.

beats.new_visual_element: A monoclonal antibody filed as a kinase inhibitor
beats.narration: Here is the error type that runs through the whole chapter. The textbook lists cetuximab among drugs that cause tyrosine kinase inhibitor keratitis. Cetuximab is a monoclonal antibody. It binds the outside of the receptor. It is not a small-molecule kinase inhibitor, and that sentence sits inside a section about kinase inhibitors. Nothing here was invented. A real drug was filed in the wrong class.

beats.new_visual_element: A row that went false after it was written
beats.narration: One row was true when the chapter was written, true when the workbook was built, and false by the time I checked it. The chapter lists pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma among cancers with no actionable targets. On the 26th of August 2026, the FDA approved daraxonrasib for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Median overall survival, 13.2 months against 6.7. That approval landed about a month before my review.

beats.new_visual_element: The correction that was itself wrong
beats.narration: Chapter 25 already had a completed workbook from an earlier pass, and re-checking it against the sources changed six of its calls. Twice, that earlier plan was going to correct the textbook when the textbook was right. The EMA really did authorise ctDNA testing for EGFR status in September 2014. The National Cancer Institute checklist really does carry 30 criteria. Flagging something true as false is also an error.

props.costLine: A fact-check can be wrong in both directions. Nobody audits the corrections.

beats.narration: Three full checks, and each one found something in my own work. The second caught five wrong first authors and a quote I had linked to a page that words it differently. The third caught nine quotations ending in a full stop the source did not have, and four statements I could not tie back to a source I had actually read. Forty-four sources in the end, every quoted fragment located in the page its link opens.

beats.new_visual_element: The viewer gets the same job
beats.narration: So here is the thing I would hand to you. Take a correction someone has already made to a document. Before you accept it, open the source it cites and check whether the original was actually wrong. Corrections can be wrong in the other direction, and almost nobody checks those.
